subject: Chemistry
description: Covers Isotopes, Plum Pudding, Gold Foil.

questions.stem: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number but a different mass number. This difference is caused by a variation in the number of:

options.option_text: Neutrons
Protons
Electrons
Positrons

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The identity of an element is determined purely by its Atomic Number (the number of protons). Isotopes of an element have the exact same number of protons (and electrons, if neutral) but differ in the number of neutrons in the nucleus. Because neutrons have mass, this changes the atomic mass number. For example, Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.
DECOY BUSTING: Changing the number of Protons creates an entirely new element. Changing the number of Electrons creates an Ion (charged atom). Positrons are antimatter equivalents of electrons, not standard components of a nucleus.
EXAM INSIGHT: Because isotopes have the same number of electrons, their chemical properties are virtually identical. However, their physical properties (like mass and radioactivity) differ. Radioactive isotopes are widely used in medicine (Cobalt-60 for cancer) and archaeology (Carbon-14 for dating).

questions.stem: Who proposed the 'Plum Pudding' model of the atom, suggesting that the atom was a positively charged sphere with negatively charged electrons embedded within it?

options.option_text: J.J. Thomson
Ernest Rutherford
Niels Bohr
John Dalton

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: After discovering the electron in 1897 using a cathode ray tube, J.J. Thomson proposed the 'Plum Pudding' model in 1904. He envisioned the atom as a diffuse cloud of positive charge (the pudding) with negatively charged electrons (the plums) scattered throughout to make the atom electrically neutral.
DECOY BUSTING: Rutherford destroyed this model with his Gold Foil experiment (proving the existence of a dense, central, positive nucleus). Bohr proposed that electrons orbit in fixed, quantized energy levels. Dalton proposed the first scientific atomic theory (atoms are indivisible solid spheres).
EXAM INSIGHT: The sequence of atomic models is a highly tested timeline: Dalton (Solid Sphere) -> Thomson (Plum Pudding) -> Rutherford (Nuclear/Planetary) -> Bohr (Quantized Orbits) -> Schrodinger (Quantum Cloud).

questions.stem: In Ernest Rutherford's famous gold foil experiment, the fact that a tiny fraction of alpha particles bounced straight back toward the source proved that:

options.option_text: The atom contains a very small, dense, positively charged nucleus at its center
Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels
The atom is entirely indivisible and solid
Neutrons exist alongside protons to stabilize the atom

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Rutherford fired heavy, positively charged alpha particles at a microscopically thin sheet of gold foil. Most passed straight through, proving the atom is mostly empty space. However, a tiny fraction (about 1 in 8,000) bounced straight back. Rutherford famously said it was like firing a 15-inch naval shell at tissue paper and having it bounce back. This proved that all the positive charge and almost all the mass of the atom is concentrated in a tiny, incredibly dense core—the nucleus.
DECOY BUSTING: Fixed energy orbits were proposed later by Bohr. Dalton's indivisible solid sphere theory was debunked by this very experiment. Neutrons were not discovered until 1932 by James Chadwick.
EXAM INSIGHT: Alpha particles are essentially helium nuclei (2 protons, 2 neutrons). Because they are positive, they were violently repelled when they scored a direct hit on the positive gold nucleus.

questions.stem: Which particle, whose discovery in 1932 resolved the discrepancy between atomic mass and nuclear proton count, was identified through beryllium bombardment experiments?

options.option_text: Neutron, discovered by James Chadwick via beryllium bombardment
Positron, discovered by Carl Anderson in cosmic ray studies
Neutrino, predicted by Wolfgang Pauli to explain beta decay energy
Electron, identified by J.J. Thomson in cathode ray tube experiments

questions.explanation: James Chadwick (1932) bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and detected a neutral particle of mass ~1 amu — the neutron. This explained why atomic masses (e.g. helium = 4 amu) far exceeded their proton count (helium has 2 protons). Positrons and neutrinos are decay-related particles; the electron had been found by Thomson decades earlier.

questions.stem: According to Bohr's model, when an electron transitions from a higher energy orbit to a lower one, the energy released is described by which relationship?

options.option_text: E = hν, where h is Planck's constant and ν is frequency of emitted light
E = mv², where m is electron mass and v is its orbital speed in the shell
E = kq²/r, where k is Coulomb constant and r is the orbital radius value
E = nh/2π, where n is the principal quantum number of the target orbit

questions.explanation: Bohr's third postulate: energy difference E₂ − E₁ = hν is emitted as a photon of frequency ν when an electron drops to a lower orbit. Option D (nh/2π) is the angular momentum quantisation formula, not energy emission — a very common mix-up in competitive exams. Option B gives kinetic energy, which is unrelated to photon emission.

questions.stem: Carbon-14 (₆C¹⁴) and Nitrogen-14 (₇N¹⁴) are classified as which type of nuclear species, and what is the defining property of that class?

options.option_text: Isotones — nuclear species sharing the same neutron count in their nuclei
Isotopes — species of the same element with identical atomic number values
Isobars — different elements sharing the same total mass number (A = 14)
Isomers — species with identical mass and proton count but different energy states

questions.explanation: C-14 has Z=6 and N=8; N-14 has Z=7 and N=7 — different elements, same mass number A=14, making them isobars. They are not isotopes (different elements). They are not isotones either: C-14 has 8 neutrons, N-14 has 7 neutrons — counts differ. Nuclear isomers have the same Z and A but differ in energy state, which is not the case here.

questions.stem: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle is expressed as Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π. Which physical interpretation correctly captures what this inequality implies for subatomic particles?

options.option_text: An electron has no definite charge distribution within the nuclear boundary
Precise position measurement disturbs momentum; both cannot be exact together
Quantum particles lack both mass and velocity below a threshold temperature
Orbital energy levels are discrete because electrons possess wavelike spin states

questions.explanation: Heisenberg's principle is a fundamental quantum property: smaller uncertainty in position (Δx) forces larger uncertainty in momentum (Δp = mΔv), and vice versa. This is not an instrument limitation but an intrinsic quantum constraint. Options A, C, and D describe unrelated phenomena — nuclear charge distribution, threshold effects, and spin quantisation — which are common distractors in MCQs conflating different quantum concepts.

questions.stem: In the quantum mechanical model, which quantum number determines the shape of an atomic orbital — distinguishing, for example, a spherical s-orbital from a dumbbell-shaped p-orbital?

options.option_text: Principal quantum number (n), which determines the energy level and shell size
Azimuthal quantum number (ℓ), which defines the orbital's angular momentum shape
Magnetic quantum number (mℓ), which fixes the orbital's spatial orientation axis
Spin quantum number (mₛ), which distinguishes the two electron spin directions

questions.explanation: The azimuthal quantum number ℓ defines shape: ℓ=0 → s (sphere), ℓ=1 → p (dumbbell), ℓ=2 → d (cloverleaf). Principal quantum number n sets energy and shell size (most common confusion with ℓ). Magnetic quantum number mℓ sets spatial orientation within a magnetic field; spin mₛ distinguishes +½ from −½ spin only.

questions.stem: A particle of mass m moves at speed v, giving it a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/(mv). If its speed is simultaneously doubled and its mass halved, the new de Broglie wavelength will be?

options.option_text: Remains exactly λ — the product mv is unchanged so wavelength is conserved
Becomes 2λ — the doubled speed doubles momentum and stretches the wavelength
Becomes λ/4 — the combined mass–speed change reduces the wavelength sharply
Becomes 4λ — the halved mass overrides the speed and quadruples the wavelength

questions.explanation: λ = h/(mv). New momentum = (m/2)(2v) = mv — identical to the original. Hence λ_new = h/(mv) = λ. Option B (2λ) ignores that mass also changed, isolating only the speed change. Option D (4λ) reverses the effect of the mass change. This problem tests whether students track the product mv as a single quantity rather than treating each variable independently.

questions.stem: The ground-state electronic configuration of Chromium (Z = 24) deviates from Aufbau predictions. Which option correctly states its configuration and the quantum-chemical reason for the deviation?

options.option_text: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ — extra stability from half-filled 3d subshell exchange energy
[Ar] 3d⁴ 4s² — standard Aufbau filling with no anomaly reported for Cr
[Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ — mandated by Pauli exclusion limiting paired electrons in 4s²
[Ar] 3d⁶ 4s⁰ — the 4s orbital empties fully to stabilise a filled 3d subshell

questions.explanation: Cr adopts [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ instead of Aufbau-predicted [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s². The half-filled 3d⁵ subshell has maximum exchange energy due to symmetric electron arrangement, lowering total energy below the paired 4s² alternative. Option C has the correct configuration but the wrong reason — Pauli exclusion permits paired 4s², it does not prohibit it. Option D would need a filled 3d¹⁰, not 3d⁶.
